sonnet.q1: A manual start: on-call runs the failover command for region B from outside A. Detection (2 of 3 outside probes see 3 failures in a row) only pages on-call. It changes no data and never fails over by itself.
sonnet.q2: If B's last recorded replay lag is over 30 s, the command stops, clears the mark and changes nothing else (A untouched), unless the operator passes the accept-data-loss override. Wait or rerun with the override. The lag is re-checked after the fence wait and the same rule applies (if it fails then, A stays fenced and B is not promoted; resume or abort).
sonnet.q3: Before promoting B: the record was `normal` and set to `failover running`, lag was at or under 30 s (or override), A was fenced (record `A fenced`, A's renewals refused, wait for lease expiry plus 10 s), and the lag re-check passed. Before B's workers start: B is promoted and accepts writes, the record is `B promoted`, running jobs are set to queued (step 6 logged), and the record is `B active` with the write lease granted to B. Before DNS moves: web tier scaled to 12, workers started, and /healthz passes on every B instance through B's load balancer.
sonnet.q4: Sessions are not copied to B (kept in Redis once per region). Users signed in at failover time must sign in again. This is accepted.
sonnet.q5: It is never used as primary again. When A returns, it is rebuilt as a replica of B. There is no automatic failback; moving back to A is a separate planned switchover.
sonnet.q6: NOT STATED as a prevention. The plan only fences via the write lease: A's apps and workers stop writing when the lease runs out, since the control store refuses renewals. The document says this does not stop the database, and a partitioned A that ignores its lease could keep writing. The plan does not yet prevent that, and it lists a network or database-level fence as an open question.
sonnet.q7: The control store (product not chosen yet), via the active-region record. It holds which region has the write lease, lease expiry, failover state and step log. The failover command writes it (state changes, fence, grant of B's lease, step log) and reads it. A's and B's apps and workers renew the lease through it every 20 s (the store refuses A's renewals when fenced). Any machine can read the step log to resume.
sonnet.q8: After B is promoted, every jobs-table row on B marked `running` is set to `queued` and its attempt count goes up by 1, before any B worker starts. These jobs restart from the beginning, so jobs must be idempotent. A side effect A made but did not record may repeat.
sonnet.q9: Resume is the default: the command continues from the last completed step in the step log, and each step checks whether it already happened. Going back to A (abort) is allowed only before promotion. Before fencing, clear the mark. After fencing but before promotion, the command confirms B is still a replica, then the operator clears `A fenced` and A's apps retake the lease. After promotion, and after DNS moves, abort is refused. Resume is the only way forward.
sonnet.q10: NOT STATED in detail. The document says only that the DNS TTL is 60 s, so most clients reach B within about a minute after DNS switches. Until DNS moves, users still reach A, which is down and fenced. Whether some resolvers ignore the TTL is an open question.
sonnet.q11: Target RPO is 30 s. It is limited by the 30 s replay-lag check (before and after fencing) unless the operator passes the accept-data-loss override. B's replica is typically under 5 s behind. Writes A makes during the fence wait count only if B received them. Writes B never got are lost. The recorded lag does not grow while A is silent, so it may understate lost writes (an open question).
